charles-williams-1885-07-04.A1:
LACK OF LAW IN LAURENS. AN INVESTIGATION OF THE RECENT OUTRAGES. A Negro Murdered by a Negro---A Suspicious Lynching--Public Opinion in Laurens C. H., Forces the Resignation of the Intendant and Wardens on Account of the Irby Case --- Milam more Scarrd than Hurt --- The Dastardly Assassination of Warren Bennett---What the People of Laurens Think about the Outrages --- The Inefficient Character of the Officers of the Law. THE NEWS AND COURTER BUREAU OAKLAND, CALIFORNIA JULY 20
On the 19th of July Alfred Dean, alias Alfred Harley, colored, shot and killed Mack Byrd, also colored. The next day Coroner Job J. Boozer held an inquest, the evidence taken being fled in the office of the Clerk of Court on July 28. The murderer had fled, but the Governor had not been notified of the result of the inquest or of the flight until the 30th of July. There was nothing remarkable about this case, and I did not investigate it further.

A Peculiar Lynching.

On the night of the Fourth of July Charles Williams, colored, who had been arrested for an alleged attempt to ravish a young white girl, was being conveyed under guard to Laurens Court House, when he was taken from the constables and shot to death in the public road, about five and a half miles from Laurens Court House. The inquest was held on the 5th inst. by Trial Justice W. B. Toddard, acting coroner, but the evidence was only filed with the Clerk of the Court on the 27th, and no report has been made to the Governor.

The evidence recorded is very brief and covers only the testimony of Constable J. A. Burdett, his assistant, Eddie Shell, and J. A. Rodgers, who found the dead body in the road. The evidence of the two first was to the effect that they were leading Williams by the rope with which he was bound; that he complained that he could hardly travel on account of the beating he had received that morning; that while he was going along and assseverating his innocence his conductors were halted by twelve or fifteen men, whose color they did not discern, although no mention of masks is recorded; that these men helped themselves to the prisoner, while he protested his innocence, and took him down the road, and that his late keepers heard shots fired and went on to Laurens. There is no mention of any resistance on the part of either guard or prisoner. Mr. Rodgers testified to finding the negro in the road shot through the head. An account of this lynching from one standpoint has already appeared in the News and Courier. The negro was stated to have been identified as one who entered the room on a young girl at night and placed his hand upon her head, but who, alarmed by her outcry, retreated precipitately. I have been informed of another side of the story. It is alleged by persons acquainted with the family that three elder sisters of the girl were of loose character, and surmised that the negro mistook her for one of them. The inference is a horrible one, but it belongs to the case and cannot be ignored.

Comment.—Lynching as a punishment for attempts upon female honor is an established and approved practice in South Carolina; but the scent evidence in this case and the soffo voice talk which one hears impress me with the opinion that there should be a more searching investigation of the facts.

The Irby Case.

The News and Courier has already published in full the Laurensville Herald's statement of both sides of the Irby matter, and it is unnecessary for me to repeat the details. It is admitted that Mr. Palmer and Col. J. L. M. Irby had words as to their relative muscle; that Col. Irby told Palmer that he declined to put himself on a level with him, but that he would furnish a man who would whip him; that he brought his negro servant, San Chapell, to town stood by with a pistol while the negro battered Palmer with his fists; that he admitted his violation of the town ordinance and expressed his willingness to be tried; that he heard that Mr. J. J. Pluss had spoken disparagingly of him, and got intoxicated on the strength of it; that he armed himself with a Winchester rifle and revolver, paraded the public square cursing and threatening his supposed enemies; that he sought Mr. Pluss and lunged at him with the muzzle of his rifle; that Mr. Pluss caught it and wrenched it from him and that he then drow his revolver and was disarmed of that also; that Mr. Pluss and Col. Irby's brother bore him to the ground and that Mr. Pluss choked him a little to subdue him, and held him down until he was taken to a carriage and conveyed to his home several miles from the town; that when sober he returned to town and readily gave two bonds for five hundred dollars each—one for assault with intent to kill and the other a peace bond—both being the result of warcouts sworn out by Mr. Pluss.

Col. Irby expressed a desire to see me and talked freely, moderately and courteously on the subject. He admitted, he said, that it was not lawful for him to knock people about, or to get a substitute to do it, but he thought that in the case of Palmer it was excusable on account of the character of the man. Palmer had made himself very obnoxious to gentlemen and was constantly embroiled. He had insulted him and dared a fight and he had selected a negro of about his size and put him to the test. His relations with Mr. Pluss had been very friendly and he had naught against him. He did not remember anything about his assault on him for he was intoxicated.

He did not admit, however, that he had in any degree sought to kill him. He desired to say that he condemned lawlessness as heartily as any man. He had himself broken the law, but he did not shirk the consequences.

"Whiskey," I suggested, "was at the bottom of the whole affair?"

"Yes" was the reply, "you are about right."

I interviewed Mr. Pluss, who is a member of a large mercantile firm, and has an excellent standing in the community. He said that Col. Irby when sober was entirely inoffensive and courteous, but when intoxicated was almost crazy. He had no feeling against him, but he had sworn out the warrants from a sense of public duty. It was a disgrace to the town that a man should be permitted to go armed about the streets, threatening and cursing and assaulting without hindrance by the authorities. He wisened the law vindicated and turbulence suppressed, once for all. He could have taken Col. Irby's own gun or pistol and killed him, but he declined to take advantage of what would have been his legal right. He intended only to bring him face to face with the law.

Mr. Palmer is not favorably regarded in Laurens. He is a Canadian, a painter by trade, and has been in the town only a few months. It is said in all quarters that he is frequently intoxicated, and that when so he is insolent to people who have said nothing to him and seeks quarrels and street fights.

Col. Irby is said to be a veritable madman when intoxicated, but at other times quiet and courteous. As to the action of the officials, Sheriff Ballew denied point blank that he was present when either assault occurred. He was the one who arrested Col. Irby at his home.

Mr. Charles Myers, the town marshal, (and the only local peace officer) is said to be a determined man. It is stated that he went to the acting intendant, Mr. F. Robertson, and asked him if he should arrest Col. Irby. The intendant was indifferent and said that he "night as well let the thing go!" At this reply the marshal pulled off his badge, put down his club and resigned. In view of the resignation of the intendant and council he was afterwards induced to serve until a new council should be elected. It is believed that he would have made the arrest promptly if authorized to do so.

The people of the town whom I talked to criticised the management of the affair very freely. Considering
charles-williams-1885-07-04.A3:
Lawlessness in Laurens. [News and (survey]
The special correspondent of the News and Courier who was sent to Laurens County a few days ago to investigate the several instances of lawlessness which have recently occurred in that county has performed the duty assigned to him, and reports, the result in a letter which we published to-day.

The inquiries of our correspondent were conducted in a careful and impartial spirit, with no other purpose than to elicit the truth, and as the information which he obtained was derived from the most trustworthy sources, there can be no question as to its substantial accuracy. It shows, moreover, that the accounts of the lawlessness in Laurens County which have already been published in the News and Courier and in the Laurensville Herald have not exaggerated either the nature of the crimes or the indifference and neglect displayed by the local authorities in failing to discharge their duty with reference to the criminals.

It is not necessary to repeat the details that have been given in regard to the assaults instigated and committed by Col. Irby upon Palmer and Pluss, respectively. There were numerous witnesses of these assaults, and both will be made the subject of a judicial investigation, the results of which may not properly be anticipated. Col. Irby is under bond to answer to the serious charges made against him, and the people of Laurens must now look to their Courts to assert and vindicate the law which he admits that he has violated. It is stated that Col. Irby is a courteous gentleman and good citizen when not under the influence of liquor, and no one should know better than himself the gravity of his offence and the necessity for its punishment. When men of his character and standing give way to violent passion and imperil the lives of their fellow-men with impunity, under whatever circumstances, it is not surprising that their example should be followed by men of lower class, who are without the restraining influence of education, personal pride and social position, and that lawlessness should prevail among them to any extent.

There is nothing to be said save in the way of strong condemnation in regard to the lynching of the negro Charles Williams, and the deliberate and hastily murder of the colored boy Warren Bennett. In the case of Williams the victim was taken from the custody of the officers of the law while carnestly protesting his innocence, and was shot dead in the public highway by the self-appointed jury and executioners. There is no hint that even a form of irregular trial was had in this case and the victim was apparently sacrifice.
in the public highway by the self-appointed jury and executioners. There is no hint that even a form of irregular trial was had in this case, and the victim was apparently sacrificed to the blind rage of his murderers, without an effort on their part to established the fact of his guilt.

In the other case, that of the killing of Bennett, the testimony so far obtained shows that the murder was one of the most atrocious crimes ever committed in this State. It should have been promptly investigated, and the delay that has already occurred in its investigation casts a deep reproach upon the responsible officials of the county. The testimony of a number of persons points clearly to one or both of two men as being concerned in the murder; their names and the circumstances which indicate their guilt are generally known and discussed in the county, but no effort was made to arrest them until sufficient time had elapsed to allow them to escape.

The story of the alleged ill treatment of the emigration agent, Milam, which was first published in an Atlanta paper, appears to have been greatly exaggerated. The truth in regard to this occurrence is, apparently, that Milam became frightened in view of the threatening demonstrations made against him and fled the county without waiting for hostilities to begin. The pistol salute which hastened his sudden departure will suggest to many persons, however, that Milam did not leave too soon for his own comfort and safety.

Our correspondent was assured, and found reason to believe, that public sentiment in Laurens County is strongly opposed to the condition of affairs which provails there, and that the law abiding people of the county appreciate the injury that must result to them if the impression obtains abroad that the county is not a safe place to live in. It is very significant, however, that the colored people of the county have so far adsorbed that impression that large numbers of them have already moved away, and that it is necessary to banish emigration agents at the point of the pistol. It is time for the law-abiding citizens to declare and enforce their sentiments when colored laborers are afraid to work in the fields alone, and when white men are afraid to testify to crimes of which they have knowledge.

In view of the facts which are presented in the letter of our correspondent it will scarcely be disputed that a state of things exists in Laurens County that should be speedily remedied. The crimes enumerated are assuredly of a character to demand the promptest and most determined action on the part of the officers of the law, but such action has
medied. The crimes enumerated are assuredly of a character to demand the promptest and most determined action on the part of the officers of the law, but such action has not been had in any instance, so far as known. Even the plainest and simplest requirements of the criminal statutes have been disregarded, and official reports of brutal murders have been pigcon-hoiled for weeks, instead of being forwarded to the State authorities for the attention they required, and which was necessary to promote the ends of justice.

The people of Laurens County are said to be fully alive to the evils described and to the necessity of a change for the better. This is well, but it is not enough. Mere sentiment will accomplish nothing unless it is expressed and enforced. The root of the trouble manifestly lies in the inefficiency of the local authorities, and the work of reform must begin with them. The people of the county owe it to themselves and to the State to turn out the men who misrepresent them in public office, and who hold so lax views of their duties. A great deal has been accomplished in fixing the blame where it belongs, and the citizens of Laurens and Governor Thompson will not fail to do the rest.

SUPPRESSING THEIR OWN RUF- FIANS.
Southern newspapers continue to speak plainly about the lawlessness in their respective neighborhoods. The Charleston News and Courier, instead of suppressing some stories of recent law breaking by alleged "gentlemen" in Laurens county, sent a special correspondent to the scene of the disturbances, printed all the details, commented severely upon all the offenders, particularly upon those of high social standing, and then put the blame where it belonged by printing the following paragraph: "Our correspondent was assured, and found reason to believe, that public sentiment in Laurens county is strongly opposed to the condition of affairs which prevails there, and that the law abiding people of the county appreciate the injury that must result to them if the impression obtains abroad that the county is not a safe place to live in. It is very significant, however, that the colored people of the county have so far absorbed that impression that large numbers of them have already moved away, and that it is necessary to banish emigration agents at the point of the pistol. It is time for the law abiding citizens to declare and enforce their sentiments when colored laborers are afraid to work in the fields alone, and when white men are afraid to testify to crimes of which they have knowledge." So many other Southern papers are speaking in a tone similar to that of the News and Courier that we may safely leave the work of reconstruction in their hands.

— Wm. McLane, of Woodberry, the driver of one of Sumwalt's ice wagons, was overcome by the heat on Wednesday. He will recover.
— A colored lad named George Brown was accidentally drowned last Sunday while bathing in the dam of the Five Mills, at Calverton.
— Emory Grove camp-meeting commences on Thursday next, 6th inst., and will be one of the largest gatherings every held upon those grounds.
— The Towson Guards' annual tournament is announced to take place at Groom's Dairy Grove, Towsontown, Tuesday, August 25th. See advertisement.
— A German carp, weighing 7 pounds and 16 ounces, was caught in the reservoir at Hampden, Monday night last. The fish measured 26 inches in length.
— The storm of Sunday afternoon last badly knocked down and tangled the oats in some sections of the county, but otherwise not much damage was done.
— Mentzel's paper mill, at Union, 1st district, is undergoing extensive repairs and new and improved machinery is being put in to increase the capacity of the mill.
— Mrs. Jonathan Disney, of Gray's Factory, 1st district, was stricken with paralysis while attending to her household duties on Sunday, and died almost immediately.
— The intensely warm weather of last week largely increased the death rate in Baltimore city, the total number of deaths having been 318, the highest within seven years.
— Mrs. Ebaugh, wife of David A. Ebaugh and daughter of Mr. John Wesley Armacost, died at her home, near Trenton, Baltimore county, on the 18th ult., aged 31 years.
— A good work horse belonging to Mr. Julius Rudiger, store-keeper, of this place, died of colic a few days ago. This is the third horse he has lost within a year by death.
— The store of Mr. R. F. Harkins, at McComas's Cross Roads, Harford county, was burned on Saturday night last, with its contents. The origin of the fire is a mystery.
— Pay clerk Charles A. Roe, of the Maryland Central railroad, went up the road on Tuesday and paid off all the hands for June. The pay roll amounted to about $6,000.
— The trustees of Woodberry public school have elected Mr. R. C. McGinn principal for the ensuing year. This school has been taught for some time by Prof. B. C. Reed, of Towsontown.
— A temperance meeting will be held on Sunday afternoon, 2d inst., at Piney Grove Church, near the 13-mile switch, P. W. & B. R. R., at which there will be addresses, readings, &c.
Elias Williams, a colored man 88 years of age, died in Baltimore a few days age. He was born in Baltimore county and was a slave of the late Richard Taylor. He was a very worthy man.
Capt. D. P. Barnette, of the Bond Guard, Catonsville, has issued an order directing the officers of his command to wear the usual badge of mourning for thirty days out of respect for Gen. Grant.
The P., W. & B. Railroad Company has raised the block signals at its stations ten or fifteen feet higher than they formerly were, which enables the engineers to see them at a greater distance.
By the destruction by lightning of the Maryland Central railroad ticket office at Baldwin station, on Sunday afternoon last, the company lost about $25 in money and light freight stored therein.
Mr. Geo. D. Hampshire, a well known resident of the upper end of the county, died at the residence of his son-in-law, Mr. John H. Harris, near Hoffmanville, 6th district, a few days ago, at an advanced age.
The annual harvest home of the Harford county farmers will be held at the Rocks of Deer Creek, Thursday and Friday, August 13th and 14th. Large numbers of Baltimore county farmers attend this gathering.
On Tuesday the County Commissioners awarded the contract for building an open wooden bridge over Stemmer's run, 12th district, to John H. Beckley for $348. There was one other bid the figures in which were $400.
No horses and carriages will be permitted to enter the Emory Grove camp-ground except on a permit signed by the president of the association. A horse pound 500 feet in length has been erected within the grounds.
John T. Wheeler, a resident of Hampden, Baltimore county, died very suddenly in Baltimore, last Sunday. He was about 45 years of age and served in the Federal army during the late war. He leaves a wife and one child.
The Senior Gunpowder Agricultural Club held its regular monthly meeting at the residence of Mr. A. C. Scott, on Saturday last. As usual the meeting proved very interesting and the members of the club had a most enjoyable time.

—St. Ann's Catholic Church, on the York road, near the Boundary, is to be considerably enlarged and improved at a cost of $13,000. The money for the purpose was left by the will of Mrs. Sally Kennedy Boone, who died some two years ago.

—On Saturday last a number of girls employed in the Clipper Mill, Woodberry, were made very sick by the terrible smell arising from Jones's falls, and which is said to be mainly caused by refuse flowing into the stream from Melvale distillery.

—A fine Jersey cow, belonging to Gen. John Gill, of Catonsville, and valued at $800, was struck by an engine on the Short-Line road, a few days ago, and had one of her legs broken besides receiving other injuries. It is thought her life can be saved.

howard-cooper-towsontown.A3:
Condemning the Cooper Lynching. HAGERSTOWN Md. July 25 About
HAGERSTOWN, Md., July 25.—About fifty colored people met at Bethel A. M. E. Church recently. Rev. William H. Brown, presiding elder of this circuit, presided; Francis Wheaton, secretary. The meeting was opened with singing and prayer by Rev. Daniel Draper. The latter made a speech on the Cooper hanging. His language was generally temperate. Rev. J. H. A. Johnson, presiding elder of Baltimore circuit, Perry Moxley and Isaiah Hatton, of this place, reported the following, which were unanimously adopted by a rising vote:

"Whereas, there is a growing spirit of lawlessness toward the colored people of the State of Maryland, which is manifested by the cruel and sudden slaying of any colored man accused of a revolting crime; Therefore be it

"Resolved, That the time has not only come, but has fully come, when the colored people of this State should assemble for the purpose of taking into consideration whatever means are necessary for their protection and promotion.

"Resolved, That the great number of colored men accused as criminals who have been lawlessly slain in this State within the last few years is a stigma upon the fair name of Maryland."

The worse than silly rumor set afloat in Towsontown on Friday of last week that a body of colored men was coming here that night to mob the town in retaliation for the lynching of Cooper, caused some little excitement and a few citizens held a meeting to consider the worst trouble on new railroads.

They were misled, of course, and they don't like to hear anything said about that meeting now. This was perhaps the most utterly absurd rumor ever set on foot here and that any one should have attached any importance to it is entirely beyond our comprehension. The whole thing was a well-concocted lie but so flimsy that any one with his wits about him should have been able to see through it at a glance.

Those Baltimore reporters who dashed out to Towsontown in hacks between 1 and 2 o'clock on Saturday morning last, to record the terrible slaughter which was to take place here that night, must have seen that somebody had played a big joke on them when they got here and found the town as quiet as Greenmount Cemetery. Some of them had the good sense to say nothing about it, but the Morning Herald man, with a desire to make a mountain out of a mole hill, strung together a lot of the most brilliant lies we have seen in print lately and published them in Saturday morning's edition, to the infinite amusement of the people of this place. Towsontown will vote that reporter a very fine leather medal, he having won the distinction of being the champion liar of the age.
howard-cooper-towsontown.A8:
Simiar to Martin Henry and Simpson Case.
Some excitement was created in Towsontown last week by the circulation of a foolish report that a large number of colored people from Baltimore and Washington had determined to attack that place for the purpose of wreaking vengeance upon the whites for the lynching of Howard Cooper. These reports originated from the sheriff having received two anonymous threatening letters, and a colored woman at Dr. Piper's another, warning her not to remain in Towsontown on that night. The colored camp in progress near that place was reported to be the place of rendezvous for the raiders, although stories of the sort had been mentioned for a week, and even in advance of the meeting of the camp. The reports were seriously entertained by but a few of our most timid citizens. That the sheriff expected an attack and that there was a white man in jail, charged with an assault on a colored woman, are denied by the sheriff. To pacify the timid, a corporal's squad was left in charge of the armory of the Towson Guards on Friday night last, but was not continued.

On Sunday of last week, Rev. W. E. Scott, president of the Conference of the African Methodist Protestant Church, and in charge of the camp-meeting, said at the public service that the reports were not true in any way whatever, and the person or parties who reported them did so with a bad design and evil heart. They are no friends to the persons holding the camp, nor to the colored people of Towsontown, nor to religion, nor to Ged, nor to anything good or decent. He knew sheriff Knight personally, and will do as much as any one to protect him in his office. We have nothing to do with Howard Cooper's case, he said, in any way, shape or form. We are here in the interest of our church. I am a man of peace and striving to keep the peace, he said in conclusion. — Towson Voice.
howard-cooper-towsontown.A9:
BRUTALITY IN MARYLAND. WHAT ARE YOU GOING TO DO ABOUT IT?
A Colored Woman Taken from the Court Room and Brutally Beaten—Another Assaulted by a White Scamp—No Arrests—Silence of the Press—Other Matters.

BALTIMORE, Aug. 10.—Miss Hannah Lubbuck of Camden, N. J., is visiting her relatives and friends here. Mrs. A. D. Parker and daughter are visiting Newport. Mrs. E. A. Akles is paying Virginia a visit. Mr. Joseph E. Johnson of the well-known firm Johnson & Bro., on Franklin street, is convalescent. Those brothers are fine men and run a first-class house. They know how to take care of the pennies. Jas. H. Coleman of Richmond, Va., died in this city a few days ago.

The 3d inst. two cowardly white brutes at Hillsboro, Caroline Co., Md., dragged Kate Brown (colored) from the Squire's office, where she was waiting their trial for having in her own house a few days before inhumanly beaten her. The second whipping was more severe than the first. Several bystanders gave the poor woman no assistance at all, while the constable slyly slipped away to Cape May, where he can do the country much valuable service by drowning himself.

Aug. 4, at Hampstead, Miss Amanda Harris, aged 17, was assaulted by one John Brummel (white). The white ox accomplished his purpose and then threatened her life if she told on him. This ox has been reported to the authorities but has not been arrested, much less lynched, while the Eastern Shore brutes are held under slight bail for appearance to court. Here is another chance for the brainless mob at Towson to show its desire to protect mothers, daughters and home. If it is unlawful to protect the chastity of colored ladies, amalgamation is also unlawful. The papers have been so quiet about these outrages that one would think nothing had happened. Thus many outrages against us are concealed. When Cooper made his assault upon that white girl the papers immediately, in their editorials, set in judgment upon him; but upon these outrages there has not been a single editorial comment, yet the Herald is the colored man's friend. We did expect a protest from the Maryland Director, but it has nothing to say in defence of its people at all. And when we consider it is edited by a minister of the gospel who has put on its first page "Uncertain in religion," we expect nothing from it, because it is too uncertain in everything. There is in it a harangue with one Bloxom about "Convention." Editors should know that this age does not appreciate and tolerate slang, vituperation and brawls. We would expect them in rum mills and other places of ill fame, but we expect editors to use reason and culture. If an editor cannot answer articles without disrobing himself of editorial graces and honor and apparently dehroning himself of reason, it is best to let them pass.

The temperance people are holding forth every Sunday at the entrance of Druidhill Park. They seem to speak with that force which is backed by strong convictions, warm hearts and clear heads. They declare they will carry their banner worldwide, making it impossible for future generations to enter a world filled with rum hells. Some of them have ostracised that archangel, Daniel, declaring that he has moved over to the side of evil. They have the same opinion of the man that many other fair-minded people have.

The American showed great grief over the death of the savior of the country, while the Sun, Herald and other papers showed very little; but as beasts without hearts are non-susceptible of grief, those papers are excusable. The Director was one-fourth in mourning, claiming to be one-fourth Republican.

"Why was no indignation meeting over the lynching of Cooper held?" seems to be foremost in every breast, and after proper time for holding it has nearly elapsed, the people are very expressive of their wonder and dislike at such a course. It would have shown race pride and a disposition at self-protection which are right and commendable, and the custom of all civilized people everywhere. It is thought there would have been a Christian protest against the barbarous act, but as outrages upon colored persons fall below the notice of Christianity, we expected race affinity to express itself. It is not supposed that such a meeting would have been attended with many surface signs of success, but it would have been putting "the seed in the earth and the leaven in the lump"

Dana, Rev. F. B. Hodges and Dr. Frear. Rev. A. R. Palmer pronounced the benediction. Rev. H. G. Miller of the Church of the Covenant preached a Grant memorial sermon a week ago last Sunday morning.

Anthracite Lodge, No. 1629, G. U. O. of O. F., will picnic at Mountain Park Wednesday, the 26th inst. The first train will leave the L. & S. depot at 8:20 A. M.

Russel, son of Mrs. Mary Brown, who had his toes cut off by the caws a short time ago, died last Friday in the 6th year of his age. The funeral took place Sunday from Bethel Church. The Rev. A. R. Palmer officiated, assisted by Revs. W. A. Ely and H. G. Miller. Interment in the city cemetery. Mr. and Mrs. Mart Thompson have lost their infant daughter, aged one week. Eliza, daughter of Oliver and Emma Downey, died last Sunday in the 10th year of her age, after a long illness. She was buried Tuesday from the residence of her parents, Rev. A. R. Palmer officiating. Interment in the city cemetery.

Rev. W. A. Ely of Zion A. M. E. Church exchanged pulpits with Rev. S. Hancock of the Primitive Methodist Church, on Sheridan street. The exchange was appreciated by both congregations. Quarterly meeting will be held at Zion Church next Sunday. The Presiding Elder of the district, Rev. John Thomas of Binghamton, N. Y., will be present.

Mrs. Isaac Gould of Pittston was the guest of Mrs. K. H. Brown Sunday evening. George and Mrs. Overton of New York arrived here this morning.
howard-cooper-towsontown.A10:
Trinity P. E. Church, Towsontown.—Preaching Sunday by the rector, Rev. W. H. H. Powers, at 11 a. m. and 7½ p. m. Bible class Wednesday at 7.45 p. m.

There will be preaching at Lutherville, by Rev. W. H. H. Powers, in the Public Hall, every Sunday afternoon, at 3½ o'clock.

St. John's Mission, York Road.—Preaching Sunday, Aug. 23d, at 3½ p. m., by Rev. Watson Case.

Prof. G. Clinton Hanna's summer normal class closed its sessions on Wednesday.

A good many Baltimore county farmers are holding back their wheat, waiting for a rise in the market.

The mill at Union, 1st district, has resumed operations with reduced wages and a reduction in the number of operatives.

The School Board will hold a meeting on Tuesday next, 25th, to confirm the teachers and for the transaction of other business.

Charles E. Jackson, Towsontown's well known barber, left on Tuesday for Chicago, where he goes on business. He will be absent several weeks.

Prospects are good everywhere for an unusually large corn crop. The growing corn never promised better at this season of the year than it does just now.

Cars on the Hampden electric railway commenced running regularly on Tuesday. The round trips are run in forty minutes, the distance being four miles.

During the heavy thunder storm on Thursday afternoon of last week the barn of John Day, near the Gunpowder, 11th district, was struck by lightning and burned.

The Pen-Mar excursion over the Maryland Central railroad on Tuesday, was largely patronized. The train contained twelve coaches and was drawn by two engines.

Emory Grove camp-meeting closed on Thursday morning last. The meetings were well attended and were successful throughout, resulting in a large number of conversions.

The annual tournament of the Towson Guards will be held at Groom's Dairy Grove, on Tuesday next, 25th instant. Extensive preparations are being made for the event.

Christian Strasinger, for fifty years a resident of Waverly, York road, died very suddenly on 7th inst., aged 82 years. He was a stonemason by trade and was a native of Germany.

The canning-house of Messrs. S. B. Silver & Bro., on Deer Creek, was destroyed by an accidental fire on Saturday last. Loss about $6,000. Insured for $5,000 in foreign companies.

The great colored camp-meeting on the Western Maryland railroad, above Owings' Mills, commenced on Thursday, 20th inst. It will be a very large camp, hundreds attending from the city.

Mr. Joseph S. Bowen, of this place, while at work rebuilding a bridge at Loch Raven a few days ago, had a finger of his right hand broken and the hand mashed by a heavy stone falling upon it.

In the Orphans' Court this week letters of administration were granted to T. G. Rutledge on the estate of William Johnson, and to Dora Grimmer on the estate of Valentine Grimmer, deceased.

Gerhardt Morrichen, a carpenter living at Hampden, 9th district, fell from a scaffold at the new Marine Hospital building, on Monday, and broke his left leg, the bone protruding through the flesh.

The bridge near Loch Raven station, on the road leading up to the gate house at the lake, was carried away by the flood of 3d inst., and travel in that direction has, in consequence, been entirely cut off.

About twenty county bridges were destroyed in Harford by the great flood of 3d inst., many of them large and costly ones. The Canton Bridge Company has been awarded the contract to rebuild all of them.

It is said that Keleher, who shot Mr. Hosshall, at Piney Hill, was a little apprehensive when brought to jail here that he might be treated in the same manner that Cooper was. But his fears were groundless.

We are now to have and opportunity to insure our property against damages from wind storms—something entirely new with us—and in view of recent events it strikes us that this is a very excellent scheme.

Two men walked all the way from Baltimore to Towsontown last Sunday to secure pieces of the sycamore tree upon which Cooper was lynched—and one of the men was formerly a resident of Towsontown, too.

A New York paper says Mr. John E. Owens's neighbors "protest against having their town, (Towsontown) near Baltimore, turned into "Towzertown," as it persistently is in the pleasant paragraphs about John."

—— Miss Kate Martin, of Baltimore, took the white veil at the Convent of Mercy, Mount Washington, on Tuesday morning last. She was dressed as a bride, in white, with orange blossoms and leng train. The ceremony was private.

—— Mr. John F. Conrey, of this place, has a large locust or digger wasp preserved in alcohol, which is now on exhibition at THE UNION office. The insect was caught a few days ago and is a perfect specimen, almost as large as a locust.

—— Politicians were out in force at Emory Grove last Sunday and there was any amount of wire-pulling done. But they (the politicians) stayed a respectful distance from the campground and in no way interfered with the services.

—— The Consolidated Gas Company is laying a main out the Frederick road to Catonsville, which place will be supplied with gas by October. When the next Legislature meets the people of that enterprising town expect to have it incorporated.

—— The County Commissioners have offered a reward of $200 for the arrest of John Rogers, colored, who brutally assaulted his sister-in-law, Nanoy Johnson, near Alberton, 2d district, on the 8th inst. Up to this time nothing has been heard of Rogers.

—— The report of County Treasurer Schone for the month of July shows cash on hand June 30th, $113,236; received during the month, $16,852.99; total, $130,088.99; disbursements during the month, $46,728.13; balance on hand August 1st, $83,360.86.

—— Mr. Berthold Hoen, brother of the Messrs. Hoen, of Waverly, Baltimore county, died in California on the 7th inst., in the 63d year of his age. He was the founder of the city of Santa Rosa, in that State, and had amassed a fortune in wine making and other business pursuits.

—— The meeting of the Democratic Executive Committee here on Tuesday brought many aspirants for office who just dropped along to see how the land lays. It is quite safe to say that some of them departed for their homes with their vanity knocked higher than Gilderoy's kite.

—— The late rains have been of incalculable benefit to grass fields and from the present outlook there will be good pasture until frost comes. This will be of great advantage to the farmers, who will not be obliged to commence feeding their stock so early as they did last fall.

A valuable Orange Blossom horse belonging to Mr. Wm. Lanahan, who occupies the Cassard property, on the York road, was found dead in a pasture lot last Sunday. Death is supposed to have resulted from heart disease. It is said Mr. Lanahan had refused $1,000 for him.

The money ($2,500) necessary to clear off the indebtedness of the Emory Grove Camp-Meeting Association was raised during the camp which has just closed, and the grounds will now be deeded to the M. E. church and will in future be managed by trustees appointed for the purpose.

Dr. C. A. Rutledge & Bro., the extensive canners, are preparing to build a store house at the same place where their warehouse is located, near Baldwin station, Maryland Central Railroad. They expect to have a regular passenger station established there by the railroad company.

On Tuesday last the annual retreat commenced at Woodstock College, and will continue until the 26th. This service is always preparatory to the ordinations and is intended for those who wish to take orders, there being forty candidates—the largest number ever ordained at any one time in this diocese.

JACKSON, TENN.
JACKSON, TENN.
A Negro Desperado Shot to Death by a Mob.
[SPECIAL TO THE APPEAL.]
JACKSON, August 20.—Night before last a mob in the Seventeenth District, this county, went to the house of William Cooper, colored, and fired several times, five shots passing through his body, killing him instantly. Jack Allison, a young white man, was also shot in the arm and lungs with a load of buckshot by the mob, either accidentally or through mistake, and will die. The first chapter in this and affair occurred a few weeks ago, when Cooper, who was a desperate negro, and is said to have killed one or two men, chased his employer, James Whitenton, out of the field and went to the house that night and called him out. He made a motion as if to draw a pistol, and Whitenton shot several times, severely wounding him. Cooper was recovering, and threatened, as soon as he was well, to kill Whitenton and all his family. The whole community became aroused, and the mobbing was the result. No arrests have been made. It is hoped matters will be settled without further bloodshed.

RELATIVE TO OUR PEOPLE THE COUNTRY OVER. Interesting Items In Condensed Form Culled From Exchanges for the Perusal of The Gazette Readers.
Judge Okey, of the Ohio Supreme bench died at Columbus, July 25.

Reports are adrift that El Mahdi fell ill on June 19, and died on June 22.

A Negro named Peter Stamps was taken from the jail at Douglassville, Ga., and lynched for outraging a little white girl.

It was the proprietor of a hotel at Pierce City, and not Prince City, Mo., which Hon. J. Milton Turner is reported to have sued for $50,000 for refusing him accommodations.

Fred Williams and Joe Turkington, Springfield colored boys, played in the woods Friday with a knife. Fred dared Joe to throw the knife at him. Joe did so, and Fred now has a fatal wound near the heart.

Colonel W. A. Pledger, having resigned his position as Surveyor of Customs of Atlanta, will retire to Athens, Ga., his home, and will in consequence sever his connection with the Weekly Defiance, the bravest paper of its kind in the South.

The Democratic Police Board, of Cincinnati, appointed Mr. Carroll as special policeman of the Cincinnati force. Mr. Carroll is the first colored man to receive such an appointment at the hands of a Democratic Board in Cincinnati.

Allen O. Myers says, referring to the Governor's respite of Murderer Griener, that if "Hoadly had been Governor of Judea in place of Pontius Pilate he would undoubtedly have postponed the crucifixion until after the fall election, and thus deprived the world of the Christian religion."

Lucien Lee, Dayton colored man, dreamed for three nights in succession that he had found a box of money under a flat stone on the Stillwater River. Was so impressed on his mind that he searched the river bank and actually found the box, he claims. It contained $752.50, which he banked. Lucien has a good reputation.

A fine Masonic flower emblem has been presented by Hon. E. P. McCabe, State Auditor of Kansas, to the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of Kansas. This emblem beautifully represents the Lodge of K. T., Chapter and Blue Lodge, and surpasses anything of the kind ever presented in the State.

There are probably a dozen colored men in New Orleans worth over $100,-000 in real estate, most of whom inherited their wealth, were always rich, and never fought their way up from slavery. A few weeks ago the Christ Church property on Canal street, the seat of the first Protestant church in the Mississippi Valley, was purchased by the Mercier Brothers for $95,000. They are now erecting upon it the finest business block in the city. It will cost over $120,000. The Merciers, who control perhaps the largest clothing business in New Orleans, and who have a hundred or more white men in their employ, are colored—true representatives of the old free people of color of New Orleans. Opposite the custom house is another row of elegant commercial buildings, also the property of a colored man, Aristides Marie, as fine a type of the colored aristocrat as one would want to see—elegant in his dress and manners, a type of a fine French gentleman.

I. L. Milan, passenger agent of the East Tennessee, Virginia & Georgia Railway, went to Waterloo County, S. C., to obtain transportation for six colored women to Arkansas. On his arrival he was advised by several to leave the place, as the white people of the county had threatened to kill the first one who attempted to induce the Negroes to leave. A short time afterwards a mob arrived at the hotel at which Mr. Milan was stopping, carried him some distance from the hotel, whipped him most brutally and compelled him to walk several miles through the woods. As they left him they advised him never again to attempt to persuade the Negroes of that vicinity to leave. In the consideration of labor the Negroes seem to be of extreme importance to the Southern whites. To their social worth and mental qualifications the Southern whites attach no importance.

MINOR NEWS NOTES.
Johan Fangman, his wife and 3-year-old son, died in Baltimore on the 26th from trichinois. The pork was eaten May 10. These are the first cases of that terrible malady known in Baltimore.

The Balignolles quarter of Paris was visited on the 25th by a fire which destroyed five blocks of buildings. The loss is not stated in the dispatches. Several lives are supposed to be lost.

During the night of the 25th eight incendiaries set fire to a number of houses in Klin, a town forty-five miles from Moscow, Russia, and property valued at 500,000 roubles was destroyed.

John Moppin, who murdered Daniels at Mound Junction, Ill., for marrying his daughter, was lynched on the 26th.

James Golden, a carriage painter, was accidentally shot and killed in a Chicago saloon by Geo. Link, the barkeeper, on the 26th.

Peter Stamps, a negro, was lynched by a mob at Douglasville, Ga., for an assault on a girl of 13.

Babcock & Andrews, brokers, Syracuse, N Y., failed on the 24th. They were short 600,000 barrels of oil which precipitated the failure. Their assets are estimated at $50,000 and the liabilities at $150,000.

The United States had 192 failures for the week ending on the 24th.

Two freight trains collided on the Illinois Central road, near Loda, Ill., on the 23d, wrecking both engines and a dozen cars, killing a ride-stealing tramp. The loss to the company will be $25,000.

On the night of the 24th the extensive tobacco factory of S. P. Lillienthal, corner of Barclay and Washington Streets, New York, was gutted by fire. The loss will reach $250,000.
The woolen mills at Cleveland, Tenn., were destroyed by fire on the 24th. The loss was $40,000; insurance $28.750. The mill employed sixty hands. It will be rebuilt.

The body of Joseph Kloety, who disappeared from Marquette, Mich., about two weeks ago, was found floating in the bay near that place, on the 23d. When last seen he was under the influence of liquor. He was 60 years old, and a mason by trade.

At Little Rock, Ark., on the 22d, J. Erber, a saloon-keeper, jumped into the river with suicidal intent. He was very successful.

A dispatch from Yarmouth, Eng., under date of the 22d, says: "A life-boat containing fifteen men started from here, this morning, to the rescue of the crew of a brigantine which was in distress. Before reaching its destination, however, the life-boat struck a sunken wreck and sank. Eight of its occupants were drowned. All of the unfortunate men were married."

Dispatches received from Assouan on the 22d, say that Maj. Grenfell has telegraphed thither that messengers from Gobra report that El Mahdi died of small-pox on June 29.

John Daniels, a resident of Mound Junction, Ill., on the Illinois Central, was married on the 22d to a Miss Dauphin, which so enraged the bride's father that he deliberately shot and instantly killed the groom. The murderer was promptly arrested.

Swan's Hotel, the Pittston Cracker factory, the Pittston Mills, and a number of other buildings at Pittston, Pa., were destroyed by fire on the 21st. The loss will reach $100,000.

On the night of the 20th a frightful explosion occurred on the South Pennsylvania Railroad, at Sheepskin Hollow Cut, one and a half miles south of Fort Littleton, Fulton County, Pennsylvania, instantly killing one Hungarian and two Italians, and probably fatally injuring John Martin, foreman, and an unknown negro. The accident is said to have occurred through the negligence of a workman in preparing the blast.

Mrs. Anna Neil, a patient in Bellevue Hospital, a private retreat for the insane at Batavia, Ill., committed suicide on the night of the 20th, by hanging, during the temporary absence of the attendant. She made a rope out of her dress. She was from Coles County, and aged 37.

Abe Deuser, an eccentric German farmer living near Bloomington, Ill., in a fit of insanity caused by domestic troubles, on the night of the 19th drove all his stock into his barn, went inside himself, and after locking the doors set fire to the place and perished in the flames.

John Gaunt, in jail at Jersey City, N. J., for the cold-blooded murder of his wife, became his own executioner on the 20th, hanging himself in his cell.

Frank Williams and Clarke Montgomery, employed on the plantation of J. Gray, near Butler, Ga., quarreled about a woman. Montgomery put rat poison on some meat, and Williams was fatally and several other men seriously poisoned.

Late on the night of the 20th the extensive establishment of the Wells & French Car and Bridge Company, Chicago, was partially destroyed by fire. The loss will reach $250,000, nearly covered by insurance.
peter-stamps-douglasville-1885-07-25.A4:
SOUTHERN NEWS GLEANINGS.
At Milledgeville, Ga., Bill Todd was convicted of the murder of a negro known as "Free Joe." The murder resulted from a quarrel over a woman. Free Joe was noted as the original of Uncle Remus, in Joel Chandler Harris' works.

CAPTAIN CHAS. J. BOARDMAN, a well-known Southern boatman, died at Bay St. Louis.

A negro committed a terrible outrage the other night on a highly respectable young white girl at Douglasville, Ga. She died next day. The negro was captured and lynched by a mob composed of leading citizens of the county.

FRANK P. KEEZE, who embezzled about $20,000 of the funds of the Rock City Building and Loan Association, of Nashville, Tenn., is thought to have joined the Canadian colony.

Three coaches on the Memphis and Little Rock Railroad were dumped into the river at Memphis, Tenn., the other night by the breaking of the incline on the Hopefield side. Nobody hurt.

The first new bale of cotton for the season of 1885 was received at Memphis on the 24th from Houston, Texas. It was consigned to Stewart, Gwynne & Co.

CAPTAIN S. S. GARRETT, Supervising Inspector of the Sixth District, died in Memphis, of diabetes, aged forty-nine years.

W. A. PRINCE, one of the most active members of the Memphis Cotton Exchange, died recently, after a lingering illness.

JEFF DAVIS pays taxes on 1,182 acres of land in the parish of Avoyelles, La.

A number of institutions in Savannah bear the name of Telfair. This is after Miss Mary Telfair, who devotes her fortune to the improvement of the city and the development of the literary and artistic tastes of the people. The latest of her observations is the Telfair Hospital for Females, which is to be opened in the autumn.

GENERAL JOSEPH E. JOHNSTON is now seventy-eight years old. His hair and beard are white as snow, save for occasional dark threads that withstand the encroachments of time. He dresses in black and wears a bell-crowned hat of light color. He is about medium height, stands erect and walks vigorously. To a Western reporter he looked as if he had some sorrow on his mind, and had the appearance of unusual reserve.

A colored man named Laws got on a spree at Atlanta, Ga., the other night, and took possession of a street car, and after severely beating the driver, he drove the lady passengers off at the point of a pistol and went careening down the street. A policeman interfered, but Laws whipped him, and went on. He finally met a young white man, placed a pistol against his stomach and threatened to kill him. The young man struck the negro just as the pistol exploded, and escaped with a serious flesh wound. The police then took the negro in charge. Laws has $5,000 in bank, and said he proposed enjoying himself. The wounded man will appear against him for attempting murder.

The extensive woolen mills of Hardwick & Parker, at Cleveland, Tenn., were destroyed by fire, entailing a loss of $40,000, only partially covered by insurance, and throwing 100 men out of work. Preparations for rebuilding on a much larger scale are making, and work will begin at once. But for the lack of a fire department in the city the mills might have been saved. As it was, at least $25,000 worth of jeans in an adjoining building was spared from the wreck.

The wheat yield in the vicinity of Franklin, Tenn., is about half a crop or less, but one field near town, W. H. Farmer's, will average twenty-five bushels to the acre. Another crop, R. J. Gordon's, averages seventeen bushels. Several others near town report fine yields. These are exceptionally good crops.

W. B. BURNETT, the young man who was arrested a few months ago on the charge of forgery, made his escape from the Pratt mines, near Birmingham, Ala., where he was working. The other night he was captured at Montgomery and has been returned to the mines.

THE barn of Wm. N. Morris, at Blowing Rock, Lenois County, N. C., was struck by lightning and destroyed. Edward Morris, aged sixteen, was fatally shocked.

A VETERINARY surgeon, from the Agricultural Department in Washington, upon examining a number of diseased cows, belonging to the herd of Timberlake & Massin, of Middletown, Frederick County, Va., pronounced the disease genuine pleuropneumonia. The cattle were immediately quarantined.

BLACKLEG is killing off the cattle of Tyler County, W. Va., by the score. No remedy effects it.

PAULDING COUNTY, Ga., has a sixteen-year-old youth who measures seven feet in height and weighs but ninety pounds.

LOUIS FOSTER.(colored), aged sixteen, of Spartansburg, S. C., was bitten by a mad dog two years ago. The other day he was attacked with hydrophobia and died next night.

AN Independent Southern Associated Press has been formed at Atlanta, Ga., with B. H. Richardson, of the Savannah Times, as President. It embraces the principle daily papers of Georgia, Florida, Alabama, North and South Carolina and Virginia. The Western Union has given the new association the same rates as the New York Associated Press.

▲ REVOLTING CHAPTER.
Atlanta, Ga., July 25.—Peter Stamps colored) was tynched last night at Douglass by a mob of five hundred men for alleged tape, committed upon Ida Abercrombie, daughter of a well-to-do white farmer. Two days ago her parents discovered that she was about to become a mother. She confessed that Stamps, who worked on the pace, was the father of her child, and said that he had a year ago outraged her and at various times since had compelled her to submit to his desires. Stamps was arrested and placed in jail. Yesterday Ida called her father and told him that she was going to die. Before help could be secured she expired in convulsions. A mob organized and the negro was taken from the Sheriff while he was trying to leave the county with him last night, and Stamps was hung to the railroad bridge. The negro said that he secured the girl's consent to do what he did. A post mortem examination showed the presence of strychnine in the girl's stomach. Her child was found to be colored. Great excitement prevails over the girl's death. It is a mystery as to whether she committed suicide.
